newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Exhausted refugees eat roots, leaves in east Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Exhausted refugees eat roots, leaves in east Zaire.

text.p: Tens of thousands of exhausted Rwandan Hutus, many of them teenagers and children, have descended on this village in eastern Zaire where many are surviving on roots and leaves.

The refugees, barred access to the nearby town of Lubutu by Zairean authorities reluctant to see new refugee camps take root on their soil, say they have been abandoned by the international community.

"We're the ones who have been forgotten by the international community," refugee spokesman Serundada Innocent told Reuters. "It's the survival of the fittest. Women and old men arrived exhausted. Those who can't reach Tingi-Tingi die on the way,."
Serundada estimated there were 120,000 refugees in and around the village on the road from the major town of Kisangani east to rebel-held territory bordering Rwanda and Burundi.

"We ought to avoid getting into a quarrel about numbers. There could be 40,000, 50,000 or 100,000, it's difficult to say at the moment," Philippe Duamelle of the U.N. Children's Fund UNICEF told Reuters.
He said urgent action was needed.
"The humanitarian catastrophe that was so feared is still in front of us. If no-one intervenes soon then we should fear the worst," he said.
UNICEF is spearheading an assessment trip to the region.
The U.N. special envoy for the Great Lakes region of Africa, Raymond Chretien, said on Thursday the need for a multinational military force there had greatly diminished.
But Serundada called for urgent help for the refugees.
The refugees, who included Burundian Hutus, fled their temporary homes in camps along the eastern border as Tutsi-led rebels seized towns and territory in the east.

Many had swollen feet. All were exhausted but there was no sign amongst of them of the feared Rwandan Hutu Interahamwe hardliners blamed for the 1994 genocide of up to a million minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus in Rwanda.
They were scavenging, hacking down trees and drawing water from a nearby stream but there was no immediate evidence of disease.
Officials in Lubutu, seven km (four miles) away, said they did not want the refugees there. "They must be put somewhere, but not here," one senior regional official commented.
Senior Zairean officers in Lubutu said soldiers from Zaire's presidential guard had driven rebels from the town of Walikale, to the south east.
They said a sustained Zairean counter-offensive had been put back because of logistical problems but would come once these had been resolved.
In Kinshasa, the government rejected a rebel offer of a ceasefire, saying its priority was to recapture lost territory.
"Sooner or later Zairean forces will be in a position to launch a counter-attack to recover the territory. There is no doubt about that," Interior Minister Kamanda wa Kamanda said.
